1Part A0:00–0:11

Lesson 1 — Code other people can read

Part A · 0:00–0:11 · Topic 3, LO3 (Learning Outcome 3)

You will be able to: Write code that a teammate can read and change safely: names, named constants, comments and docstrings, small functions, code review, pair programming and clean commits.

Why readable code is an engineering requirement 0:00–0:02Slide 4

Today your product starts to run. In the first part of the hour we look at the code itself: how to write it so that other people can read it. The next three parts are about testing — the five types of testing, how to design test cases from the specification and from the code, and how to write a test before the code. Everything you hear today, you use in the Studio this afternoon, in Lab 07.

Start with a fact about software work. A line of code is written once and read many times: by its author a week later, by the reviewer, by the teammate who corrects a defect in December, by the person who maintains the product next year. A field study of 78 professional developers, published in 2018 in the journal IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Software Engineering by Xia and colleagues, measured that understanding existing code took about 58 % of their working time. The official Python style guide, PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python code), starts from the same observation: code is read much more often than it is written.

Readability is therefore not a question of taste. It is a property of the product, like correctness, and it has a measurable cost: code that is hard to read takes longer to change, and a change made by someone who misunderstood the code introduces new defects.

Teams control readability with rules. A coding standard is the written set of rules for names, layout, comments and the use of language features that every member of a team follows. A style guide is a coding standard published for a whole language community: PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python code)↗ for Python, the Google Style Guides↗ for Java, JavaScript, C++ and other languages. Your team chooses one in section 0 of the Brick 7 file and follows it.

Names that say what they mean 0:02–0:05Slide 5

The first rule is about identifiers — the names you give to variables, functions, classes and constants. A good name tells the reader what the thing holds or does, so that no comment is needed to explain it.

Four conventions cover most cases. A variable or a constant gets a noun that describes its content, with the unit when there is one: days_late, fee_in_dollars. A function gets a verb phrase that describes its action: compute_late_fee, send_reminder. A Boolean gets a yes-or-no question: is_overdue, has_room. A class gets a noun: Loan, Booking.

PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python code) adds the spelling: snake_case — lowercase words joined by underscores — for functions and variables; CapWords for classes; UPPER_CASE for constants; four spaces per indentation level; and at most 79 characters per line, so that two files fit side by side on one screen.

The second rule is about numbers. A magic number is a literal number in the code whose meaning is not written anywhere — for example 0.5 or 10 in the middle of a calculation. Replace it with a named constant: DAILY_LATE_FEE = 0.50. Three things improve at once: the reader sees the meaning, a search finds every use, and when the rule changes, the value changes in one place. In Class 6 you saw one rule written in five places; a named constant prevents exactly that.

Avoid single letters, except a loop counter such as i in a three-line loop; abbreviations that only the author understands, such as clc_fee; names that state something false, such as loan_list for a dictionary; and numbered names such as data2. Inside one project, consistency matters more than any single rule: if the code base says customer, do not introduce client.

Comments that explain why, docstrings that explain what 0:05–0:07Slide 6

A comment is text that the interpreter or compiler ignores; it exists only for human readers. A useful comment explains why the code is written this way: a reason, a constraint, the requirement it implements, a decision that is not obvious. A useless comment repeats what the next line already says. x = x + 1 # add one to x gives the reader nothing. # FR-06: the fee is capped at 10 dollars per loan tells the reader where the rule comes from and which requirement to check before changing it.

Comments must change when the code changes. A comment that describes the old behaviour is worse than no comment, because the reader believes it. Reviewers check comments as carefully as code.

A docstring is a string literal written as the first statement of a module, function, class or method. Python keeps it with the object: help(), editors and documentation generators show it. The conventions are in PEP 257 (Python Enhancement Proposal 257, the docstring conventions): a one-line summary that ends with a period; for longer docstrings, a blank line and then the details — the parameters, the return value, the exceptions, the requirement. Java has the same idea in Javadoc comments, JavaScript in JSDoc comments.

A note about the demonstration programs of this course: in them, every line of code has a comment above it. That is a teaching format for beginners, so that you can follow each step. In production code you comment the reasons, not every line.

Small functions that do one thing 0:07–0:08Slide 7

A function should do one task at one level of detail. A simple check: if you need the word “and” to name it — `validate_and_save_and_notify` — split it. This is the cohesion you met in Class 6, applied to a single function.

Return early when a special case is settled — a guard clause — instead of nesting if inside if. Keep each function short enough to read without scrolling. And do not copy a block of code to a second place: apply the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle and call one function from both places.

Two kinds of tools enforce the standard for you. A linter reads the source code without running it and reports violations of style rules and likely mistakes — Ruff↗ or Flake8↗ for Python, ESLint↗ for JavaScript, Checkstyle↗ for Java. A formatter rewrites the layout automatically — Black↗ for Python. Run them before every commit; in Class 10 your continuous-integration pipeline runs them at every push.

Code review, pair programming and clean commits 0:08–0:11Slide 8

Readability is checked by a second person. In a code review, a teammate reads a change before it is merged into the main branch, using a short checklist: Is it correct? Is it readable? Is it tested? Does it follow the design and the coding standard? The reviewer writes comments, the author answers or corrects, and the reviewer approves.

On GitHub, review happens in a pull request — a request to merge the commits of one branch into another. The pull request keeps the change, the conversation and the approval together, so the team can see later why the code looks the way it does (GitHub Docs — Pull request reviews↗). Reviews find problems that tests do not show — an unclear name, a missing case, a requirement read the wrong way — and they spread knowledge: after a review, two people know that part of the code. Keep each change small; Google's code-review guide↗ asks for small changes because they are reviewed faster and more thoroughly.

Pair programming is review while the code is written. Two developers share one computer: the driver types; the navigator reads every line as it appears, checks it against the requirement and thinks about the next step. They swap roles often — in the Studio, every ten minutes. It is one of the XP (Extreme Programming) practices you met in Class 4. In an experiment at the University of Utah, reported by Alistair Cockburn and Laurie Williams in 2000, pairs used about 15 % more programmer time than individuals, and their programs had about 15 % fewer defects.

Finally, the history of the code. A commit records one change with a message. Commit hygiene means: one logical change per commit; the tests pass before you commit; and a message with a short summary line — about 50 characters, in the imperative mood, Add late-fee cap for FR-06, not fixed stuff — then a blank line and a paragraph that explains why. These are the guidelines of the Pro Git book↗. Never commit passwords or real personal data: fictional data only (Legal Notice, section 6.7 (data and privacy — fictional data only)↗).

Now the Try-it. On the screen are seven lines of a real-looking function. In pairs, you have three minutes: rename everything and remove the magic numbers. Then one pair reads its version aloud.

In pairs, three minutes: rewrite the seven lines below so that a stranger can read them — rename every identifier and replace every magic number with a named constant. One pair reads its version aloud; then the professor shows the reviewed version from the real-life example.

def f(d, r, x):
    # calculate
    if (r - d).days > 0:
        y = (r - d).days * 0.5
        if y > 10: y = 10
        return y
    else: return 0

Real-life example — ClubLend

ClubLend (Team Owl) — make the late-fee rule readable, then review it

The task this example doesRewrite a working but unreadable late-fee function so that it follows the team's coding standard, check it with a five-item review checklist, prove that its behaviour has not changed, and record the change in one clean commit.
How it relates to this lessonApplies Lesson 1 directly: identifiers, named constants instead of magic numbers, a docstring with the requirement, one task per function, a code review in a pull request, and commit hygiene.

ClubLend lets a student club lend equipment to its members. Requirement FR-06 (functional requirement 06) of Team Owl's Brick 5 says: “An item returned after its due date costs $0.50 per day late, up to $10.00 per loan.”

Maya, the Builder, wrote the first version late in the evening. It gives the right numbers, but Theo, the reviewer, cannot tell from the code what f, d, r, x and y are, where 0.5 and 10 come from, or why x is passed at all. He asks for changes in the pull request before he approves. All names and data are fictional.

First version (Maya)
def f(d, r, x):
    # calculate
    if (r - d).days > 0:
        y = (r - d).days * 0.5
        if y > 10: y = 10
        return y  # the fee that the member has to pay when the borrowed item comes back late
    else: return 0
Reviewed version
DAILY_LATE_FEE = 0.50   # dollars per day late (FR-06)
MAX_LATE_FEE = 10.00    # cap per loan (FR-06)


def compute_late_fee(due_date, returned_date):
    """Return the late fee in dollars for one loan (FR-06)."""
    days_late = (returned_date - due_date).days
    if days_late <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return min(days_late * DAILY_LATE_FEE, MAX_LATE_FEE)
Step by step
  1. Review the first version against the checklist. Theo's five rules give eleven findings in seven lines: six findings of one-letter names (f, d, r and x on line 1, y on lines 4 and 5); two magic numbers (0.5 and 10); one line of 93 characters, longer than 79; no docstring; and an unused parameter x.
  2. Rename. f becomes compute_late_fee, d and r become due_date and returned_date, y becomes days_late times the fee; the unused x is removed.
  3. Name the constants. DAILY_LATE_FEE = 0.50 and MAX_LATE_FEE = 10.00 are defined once, at the top of the module, with a comment that cites FR-06 (functional requirement 06).
  4. Add the docstring and a guard clause. The docstring states the rule and the requirement; if days_late <= 0: return 0.0 handles the on-time case first, so the main calculation is not nested.
  5. Prove that the behaviour has not changed. The same three loans — returned on time, 6 days late, 25 days late — give $0.00, $3.00 and $10.00 with the old and the new version.
  6. Commit and ask for approval. One commit with a 47-character summary line and a paragraph that explains why; Theo re-reviews: five of five checklist items pass.

Run the example — Demo 1 — a small code reviewer for ClubLend's late fee

Demo 1 — a small code reviewer for ClubLend's late fee · Python, 467 recorded steps

The task this program does: Reviews two versions of ClubLend's late-fee function — Maya's first version and the reviewed one — against five rules of the team's coding standard, prints every finding, and then runs both versions on three loans to prove that the behaviour did not change.

How it relates to the lecture: Lesson 1: names, magic numbers, the 79-character limit of PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python code), docstrings and unused parameters — the checks a linter or a reviewer makes; and the rule of every refactoring: readability changes, results do not.

1# =============================================================================
2# CS 330 · Class 7 · Lesson 1 — Demo 1: a small code reviewer for ClubLend
3# TASK: review two versions of ClubLend's late-fee function, FR-06 (functional
4# requirement 06), against five rules of the team's coding standard, then
5# prove that the readable version computes exactly the same fees.
6# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 1 — identifiers, magic numbers, line length
7# (PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python
8# code)), docstrings and unused parameters,
9# checked automatically the way a linter or a reviewer checks them; the
10# behaviour must not change, exactly as in a refactoring.
11# Fictional people and data only (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, section 6.7).
12# Runs with Python 3.10 or newer and needs no extra package.

16# in a line of text.
17import re
18
19# Import the date type, so that we can create the due date and the return date
20# of a loan.
21from datetime import date
22

24# text, not running code.

27 # parameters have one-letter names.
28 "def f(d, r, x):",
29 # Line 2: a comment that says only "calculate"; it gives the reader no
30 # reason and no rule.
31 " # calculate",

33 # days late).
34 " if (r - d).days > 0:",

44 "borrowed item comes back late",
45 # Line 7: the on-time case, written after "else" on the same line.
46 " else: return 0",
47 # The closing bracket ends the list of the seven lines of the first
48 # version.
49]

52AFTER = [

54 # the requirement.
55 "DAILY_LATE_FEE = 0.50 # dollars per day late (FR-06)",
56 # Line 2: a second named constant replaces the magic number 10.
57 "MAX_LATE_FEE = 10.00 # cap per loan (FR-06)",
58 # Lines 3 and 4: two blank lines separate the constants from the function,
59 # as PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for
60 # Python code) asks.
61 "",
62 # (Line 4 is the second blank line.)
63 "",
64 # Line 5: the function name is a verb phrase; the parameter names say what
65 # each date is.
66 "def compute_late_fee(due_date, returned_date):",
67 # Line 6: the docstring states what the function returns and which
68 # requirement it implements.
69 ' """Return the late fee in dollars for one loan (FR-06)."""',
70 # Line 7: the number of days late gets its own, descriptive name.
71 " days_late = (returned_date - due_date).days",
72 # Line 8: a guard clause handles the on-time case first, so the main
73 # calculation is not nested.
74 " if days_late <= 0:",
75 # Line 9: on time or early: no fee.
76 " return 0.0",
77 # Line 10: the fee per day, limited by the cap — one readable line instead
78 # of three.
79 " return min(days_late * DAILY_LATE_FEE, MAX_LATE_FEE)",
80 # The closing bracket ends the list of the ten lines of the reviewed
81 # version.
82]
83
84# The maximum line length that PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8) allows.
85MAX_LINE = 79
86# The findings of the review of the first version; the picture on the right
87# reads this list.
88findings_before = []
89# The findings of the review of the reviewed version.
90findings_after = []
91# The results of the behaviour check (old fee, new fee, equal or not) for each
92# loan.
93checks = []
94# The current stage of the demo, shown above the picture.
95stage = "start"
96
97
98# review() applies the five rules to a list of code lines and appends every
99# finding to "found".
100def review(lines, found):
101 # Look at the lines one by one; "number" counts from 1, as editors do.
102 for number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
103 # Remove the comment part: everything after "#" is ignored by rules 2
104 # and 3.
105 code = line.split("#")[0]
106 # Remove the text inside quotes, so that a reference such as FR-06
107 # (functional requirement 06) in a docstring is not read as a number.
108 code = re.sub(r'"[^"]*"', "", code)
109 # Rule 1 — long line: PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the
110 # official style guide for Python code) allows at most 79 characters
111 # per line.
112 if len(line) > MAX_LINE:
113 # Record the finding with the line number, the rule and the
114 # measured length.
115 found.append(
116 {
117 "line": number,
118 "rule": "long line",
119 "detail": f"{len(line)} characters",
120 }
121 )
122 # A line that starts by defining an UPPER_CASE name is a named
123 # constant: its number is allowed.
124 is_constant = re.match(r"\s*[A-Z_]+\s*=", line) is not None
125 # Rule 2 — magic number: find every different number written in the
126 # code part of the line.
127 for number_text in sorted(set(re.findall(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b", code))):
128 # 0 and 1 are not counted: their meaning is almost always obvious.
129 if float(number_text) not in (0.0, 1.0) and not is_constant:
130 # Record the magic number that the reviewer would ask to name.
131 found.append(
132 {
133 "line": number,
134 "rule": "magic number",
135 "detail": number_text,
136 }
137 )
138 # Rule 3 — short name: collect the names assigned on this line (the
139 # word before a single "=").
140 names = re.findall(r"(\w+)\s*=(?!=)", code)
141 # On a "def" line, the function name and its parameters are names too.
142 signature = re.match(r"\s*def\s+(\w+)\((.*)\)", code)
143 # If this line defines a function, add its name and its parameter
144 # names.
145 if signature:
146 # The function name, then each parameter name with its spaces
147 # removed.
148 names += [signature.group(1)] + [
149 p.strip() for p in signature.group(2).split(",")
150 ]
151 # Check each name once.
152 for name in sorted(set(names)):
153 # A one-letter name says nothing about what it holds.
154 if len(name) == 1:
155 # Record the name that should be renamed.
156 found.append(
157 {"line": number, "rule": "short name", "detail": name}
158 )
159 # Rules 4 and 5 apply only to lines that define a function.
160 if signature:
161 # The lines that follow the "def" line, without blank lines.
162 body = [text.strip() for text in lines[number:] if text.strip()]
163 # Rule 4 — no docstring: the first line of the body must start with
164 # three quotes.
165 if not body or not body[0].startswith('"""'):
166 # Record the missing docstring.
167 found.append(
168 {
169 "line": number,
170 "rule": "no docstring",
171 "detail": signature.group(1),
172 }
173 )
174 # Rule 5 — unused parameter: a parameter that never appears in the
175 # body is not needed.
176 for parameter in [
177 p.strip() for p in signature.group(2).split(",")
178 ]:
179 # Search the body for the parameter as a whole word.
180 if not any(
181 re.search(rf"\b{parameter}\b", text) for text in body
182 ):
183 # Record the unused parameter.
184 found.append(
185 {
186 "line": number,
187 "rule": "unused parameter",
188 "detail": parameter,
189 }
190 )
191 # Return the number of findings, for the summary.
192 return len(found)
193

195# Stage 1: review the first version.
196stage = "review the first version"
197# Apply the five rules to BEFORE.
198total_before = review(BEFORE, findings_before)
199# Print every finding of the first version.
200for item in findings_before:
201 # One line per finding: line number, rule, detail.
202 print(f"BEFORE line {item['line']}: {item['rule']} ({item['detail']})")
203
204# Stage 2: review the reviewed version.
205stage = "review the reviewed version"
206# Apply the same five rules to AFTER.
207total_after = review(AFTER, findings_after)
208# Print the two totals side by side.
209print(
210 f"Findings: first version {total_before}, reviewed version {total_after}"
211)

213# Stage 3: prove that the behaviour did not change — refactoring must keep
214# every result.
215stage = "check the behaviour"
216# An empty dictionary that will receive the old function when its text is
217# executed.
218old_space = {}
219# exec() runs Python code given as text: the code we reviewed is exactly the
220# code we run.
221exec("\n".join(BEFORE), old_space)
222# A second empty dictionary for the new version.
223new_space = {}
224# Run the text of the reviewed version, which defines the constants and the new
225# function.
226exec("\n".join(AFTER), new_space)
227# Take the old function out of its dictionary.
228old_fee = old_space["f"]
229# Take the new function out of its dictionary.
230new_fee = new_space["compute_late_fee"]
231# Three fictional loans: on time, 6 days late, and 25 days late (which reaches
232# the cap).
233LOANS = [
234 ("returned on time", date(2026, 11, 3), date(2026, 11, 3)),
235 # The second loan comes back 6 days after its due date.
236 ("6 days late", date(2026, 11, 3), date(2026, 11, 9)),
237 # The third loan comes back 25 days late: 25 × 0.50 = 12.50, capped at
238 # 10.00.
239 ("25 days late", date(2026, 11, 3), date(2026, 11, 28)),
240]
241# Compute both fees for each loan.
242for label, due, returned in LOANS:
243 # The old function needs its unused third parameter, so we pass None.
244 before_value = old_fee(due, returned, None)
245 # The new function needs only the two dates.
246 after_value = new_fee(due, returned)
247 # Record the comparison for the picture.
248 checks.append(
249 {
250 "loan": label,
251 "before": before_value,
252 "after": after_value,
253 "same": before_value == after_value,
254 }
255 )
256 # Print the comparison with two decimals.
257 print(
258 f"{label:17} before {before_value:5.2f} "
259 f"after {after_value:5.2f} same: {before_value == after_value}"
260 )
261
262# Stage 4: the verdict of the review.
263stage = "done"
264# The change is accepted only if no rule is broken and every result is
265# unchanged.
266approved = total_after == 0 and all(item["same"] for item in checks)
267# Print the reviewer's decision.
268print("Review decision:", "approve" if approved else "request changes")

Step-by-step explanation
  1. The two imports at the top bring two tools: re, which finds patterns such as numbers and names in text, and date, which builds the dates of a loan.
  2. BEFORE and AFTER hold the two versions as lists of text lines. A reviewer reads text, so the program reads text too; each line of each list has its own comment.
  3. review() looks at every line. It removes comments and quoted text first, so that the requirement number inside a docstring is not mistaken for a magic number.
  4. Rule by rule: a line longer than 79 characters; a number other than 0 or 1 outside a named-constant line; a one-letter name; a def without a docstring; a parameter never used in the body. Each finding is appended to a list — watch it grow in the picture.
  5. The first version gives eleven findings in seven lines; the reviewed version gives none.
  6. exec() runs the very text that was reviewed, so the program can call the old function f and the new compute_late_fee.
  7. Three fictional loans — on time, 6 days late, 25 days late — give 0.00, 3.00 and 10.00 with both versions: the behaviour is unchanged.
  8. The decision is “approve” only when no rule is broken and every result is the same — the two conditions of a good review.

Five flash-cards — turn each one

coding standard and style guideclick or press Enter to turn
A coding standard is a team's written set of rules for names, layout, comments and language features. A style guide is a coding standard published for a whole language — PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the official style guide for Python code) for Python, the Google style guides for Java, JavaScript, C++ and others.
magic numberclick or press Enter to turn
A literal number in the code whose meaning is not written anywhere (0.5, 10). Replace it with a named constant (DAILY_LATE_FEE = 0.50): the meaning becomes visible, a search finds every use, and a change happens in one place.
comment versus docstringclick or press Enter to turn
A comment is ignored by the interpreter and should explain why (a reason, a constraint, a requirement). A docstring is the first string of a module, function or class; help() and editors show it; it states what the code does, its parameters and its result (PEP 257 (Python Enhancement Proposal 257, the docstring conventions)).
code review and pull requestclick or press Enter to turn
In a code review a teammate reads a change before it is merged, with a checklist: correct, readable, tested, consistent with design and standard. On GitHub it happens in a pull request — a request to merge one branch into another, where the change, the comments and the approval are kept together.
commit hygieneclick or press Enter to turn
One logical change per commit, tests passing before the commit, and a message with a summary line of about 50 characters in the imperative mood (“Add late-fee cap”), a blank line, then why the change was made (Pro Git guidelines).

2Part B0:15–0:26

Lesson 2 — Testing fundamentals and the five types of testing

Part B · 0:15–0:26 · Topic 3, LO3 (Learning Outcome 3)

You will be able to: Tell verification from validation, name the five types of testing of LO3 (Learning Outcome 3) with what each one checks, who runs it and when, and write a test plan with measurable entry and exit criteria.

What testing can and cannot do 0:15–0:17Slide 13

Software testing is the execution of a program, or of a part of it, with selected inputs, and the comparison of its actual behaviour with the behaviour the specification requires — in order to find defects and to measure how far the product can be trusted. The reviews of Lesson 1 check code without running it; testing runs it.

Three words describe what testing looks for, in the order used by the Foundation Level syllabus of the ISTQB (International Software Testing Qualifications Board)↗. An error is a human mistake — for example, a developer reads “at least 10 minutes” as “more than 10 minutes”. The error produces a defect, also called a fault or a bug: the incorrect code, here > written where >= was needed. When the defective code runs with the triggering value, the user sees a failure — observable wrong behaviour: a student is refused a cancellation at exactly 10 minutes before the slot. A defect does not always cause a failure; it causes one only when an input reaches the defective line with a value that triggers it.

This tells us what testing can and cannot do. Edsger Dijkstra pointed out in 1970 that tests can show the presence of defects but cannot prove their absence. A test suite is a sample of all possible inputs, so the quality of testing depends on how well the sample is chosen — the subject of Lessons 3 and 4. And the earlier a defect is found, the less it costs: a defect corrected while the code is written costs minutes; the same defect found by users after release costs a report, an investigation, a correction, a new release and the users' trust.

Verification and validation 0:17–0:19Slide 14

Two words organise all checking activities. Verification asks: are we building the product right? It checks each work product against its specification — the design against the requirements, the code against the design, the running product against the SRS (Software Requirements Specification). Reviews and unit, integration and system tests are verification.

Validation asks: are we building the right product? It checks the product against the real needs of its users, in their environment. User acceptance testing, prototypes shown to users and trial use are validation. Barry Boehm gave the two questions this short form in 1979.

A product can pass every verification and still fail validation: every requirement is met, but the requirements missed what the users needed. That is why the elicitation of Class 5 matters for testing too: only the users can confirm that the requirements describe what they need.

The five types of testing 0:19–0:23Slide 15Slide 16

Learning outcome 3 of this course names five types of testing. They differ in what is tested, who tests, when, and in which environment.

Unit testing checks one function, method or class in isolation. Developers write unit tests together with the code and run them at every change; each test takes milliseconds. Example: streak_length() returns 3 for check-ins on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

Integration testing checks the interfaces and the interactions between units or components — the controller with the rules and the repository, the product with an external service. Parts can be joined all at once, which is called big-bang integration, or incrementally: top-down, with stubs in place of lower modules that are not ready, or bottom-up, with drivers that call the modules under test. The loss of the Mars Climate Orbiter↗ of NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) in 1999 is the classic interface defect. The investigation board↗ found that a ground software file produced thruster impulse in English units, pound-force seconds, while the navigation software that used it expected metric units, newton-seconds, the SI (International System of Units) unit (news release of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory↗). The interface specification required metric units, and the ground software did not follow it: the defect was in the interface between the two programs.

System testing checks the complete, integrated product, end to end, against the SRS (Software Requirements Specification) — the functional and the non-functional requirements — in an environment as close to production as possible, often called staging. Testers outside the development pair run it, often with tools such as Playwright↗ or Selenium↗ that drive a real browser. Example: register, create a habit, check in on seven days, and see 7 of 7 in the weekly report.

User acceptance testing, UAT (user acceptance testing), lets real users or the client confirm that the product supports their tasks in their setting; its result decides whether the product is accepted. It is mainly validation. When it is done at the developer's site it is called alpha testing; at the users' sites, beta testing.

Performance testing measures response time, throughput and the use of resources under a defined load, against a non-functional requirement. A load test applies the expected peak — 200 students opening their weekly report on Sunday evening. A stress test goes beyond the expected load until the system fails, to see how it fails and whether it recovers. Tools such as Locust↗, Apache JMeter↗ and Grafana k6↗ generate the load.

The first four types are also called test levels: the scope grows from one unit to the whole product, used by its real users. Performance testing is a non-functional type that is usually run at system level. And at every level, regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to check that what worked still works — which is why tests are automated.

The V-model: each level checks one specification 0:23–0:24Slide 17

You met the V-model in Class 3. Its right side is the testing we just described, and each level checks one document of the left side: unit tests check the detailed design; integration tests check the architecture and its interfaces; system tests check the SRS (Software Requirements Specification); acceptance tests check the users' needs, written as use cases and user stories.

The important consequence: tests are designed on the left, when each document is written, and run on the right. The verification lines and the alternative flows you wrote in Brick 5 are already acceptance and system test cases.

Test strategy, test plan, entry and exit criteria 0:24–0:26Slide 18

A test strategy is the general approach to testing: which types of testing are used, in which order, with which techniques, how much is automated, and what is measured. A test plan applies the strategy to one project or one version. Part 3 of the standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 (the joint software-testing standard of the International Organization for Standardization, the International Electrotechnical Commission and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)↗ defines the full content of test documentation; the Brick 7 template asks for six parts on one page.

First the scope: what is tested in this version, and what is not. Then each of the five types with who runs it and when. Then the tools and environments. Then the entry criteria — the conditions that must hold before a test activity may start, for example “the requirement has a verification line and the code is committed”. Then the exit criteria — the conditions under which an activity is finished and the version may be released, for example “all unit tests pass, branch coverage of the rules module is at least 80 %, and no severity-1 defect is open”. Finally the defect process: where defects are recorded and how a correction is checked.

Exit criteria must be measurable. “We tested enough” is not a criterion; “branch coverage ≥ 80 %” is, because anyone can check it with a tool and get the same answer.

Now the Visualize-it. Everyone draws the V-model from memory and writes the five types of testing on the right side. Where does performance testing go? Compare with your neighbour.

👁 Active Break · Visualize-it · 0:26–0:30 — Draw the V-model and place the five types

On paper, from memory: draw the V-model — the users' needs, the requirements (the SRS (Software Requirements Specification)), the architecture and the detailed design down the left side, the code at the bottom — and write the five types of testing on the right side, each opposite the document it checks. Real-life example — HabitHub

HabitHub (Team Wren) — Test Plan v1 for the streak feature, and the exit check at the end of the sprint

The task this example doesWrite the one-page Test Plan v1 for HabitHub's streak story — scope, the five types of testing with who and when, tools, entry and exit criteria, defect process — then use the exit criteria, with the team's real numbers, to decide whether the version may be tagged.
How it relates to this lessonApplies Lesson 2: the five types of testing of LO3 (Learning Outcome 3), verification and validation, the V-model, and a test plan with measurable entry and exit criteria.

HabitHub tracks daily habits. Requirement FR-02 (functional requirement 02) of Team Wren says: “The system shall show the current streak: the number of consecutive days, up to today, on which the habit was checked, counted in the student's own time zone.” NFR-02 (non-functional requirement 02) says: “The weekly report page shall load in 2 seconds or less for 95 % of requests with 200 concurrent users.”

Ana (Coordinator), Kofi (Tester), Lea (Builder) and Sam (Scribe) fill the test-plan table of the Brick 7 template on Tuesday, and check the exit criteria on Friday and again on Sunday, before tagging. All names, numbers and data are fictional.

Part of Test Plan v1HabitHub (Team Wren)
ScopeIn: streak calculation (FR-02 (functional requirement 02)), daily check-in (FR-01 (functional requirement 01)), weekly report (FR-04 (functional requirement 04)). Out, for now: reminders (FR-05 (functional requirement 05), Sprint 2) and account deletion.
Types — who and whenUnit: each pair, at every commit, now · Integration: controller + streak rules + repository, Kofi, Sprint 2 (from November 24) · System: the whole app on the staging host, run by Team Lynx, December 8 · User acceptance: two students of another team use HabitHub for one week, December 8–15 · Performance: 200 simulated users with Locust against NFR-02 (non-functional requirement 02), Lea, December 15.
Toolspytest and pytest-cov (unit and coverage), Locust (performance, later), GitHub Issues (defects).
Entry criteriaThe requirement has a verification line in Brick 5; the code is committed and passes the linter; for integration: the unit tests of the joined parts pass.
Exit criteria (this version)All unit tests pass · branch coverage of streaks.py ≥ 80 % · no open severity-1 defect · every functional requirement in scope has at least one test.
Defect processOne GitHub issue per defect with the labels bug, severity: 1/2/3, priority: high/medium/low; the correction comes with the test that exposed the defect; Kofi verifies and closes.
Step by step
  1. Fill the six parts of the plan on Tuesday, in the Studio (table above). Every type of testing gets a person and a date, even when the date is in December.
  2. Mark what this version verifies. Only unit testing runs now; the plan says when the other four types run — each type has a person and a date that anybody can check.
  3. Friday — check the exit criteria. 13 of 14 unit tests pass; branch coverage is 16 of 25 outcomes = 64 %; one severity-1 defect is open; FR-04 (functional requirement 04) has no test. All four criteria fail: no tag.
  4. Correct and add tests. The time-zone defect gets a failing test first, then the correction; two tests are added for the weekly report.
  5. Sunday — check again. 17 of 17 pass; branch coverage 22 of 25 = 88 %; no severity-1 defect open; every functional requirement in scope is tested. All four criteria hold: the team tags block7-draft.

116# check_exit() evaluates the four exit criteria for the numbers of one day.
117def check_exit(numbers):
118 # Start each day with an empty list of rows.
119 gate_rows.clear()
120 # Criterion 1: every unit test passes.
121 all_pass = numbers["tests_passed"] == numbers["tests_total"]
122 # Record the criterion, its result and the measured value.
123 gate_rows.append(
124 {
125 "criterion": "all unit tests pass",
126 "ok": all_pass,
127 "value": f"{numbers['tests_passed']} of {numbers['tests_total']}",
128 }
129 )
130 # Criterion 2: branch coverage = executed outcomes ÷ all outcomes × 100.
131 coverage = 100 * numbers["branches_hit"] / numbers["branches_total"]
132 # Record whether the coverage reaches the minimum of the plan.
133 gate_rows.append(
134 {
135 "criterion": "branch coverage ≥ 80 %",
136 "ok": coverage >= MIN_BRANCH_COVERAGE,
137 "value": f"{coverage:.0f} %",
138 }
139 )
140 # Criterion 3: no severity-1 defect may be open.
141 no_sev1 = numbers["sev1_open"] == 0
142 # Record the number of open severity-1 defects.
143 gate_rows.append(
144 {
145 "criterion": "no open severity-1 defect",
146 "ok": no_sev1,
147 "value": f"{numbers['sev1_open']} open",
148 }
149 )
150 # Criterion 4: every functional requirement in scope has at least one test.
151 untested = [
152 fr for fr in numbers["in_scope"] if fr not in numbers["tested"]
153 ]
154 # Record the requirements that still have no test (an empty list means the
155 # criterion holds).
156 gate_rows.append(
157 {
158 "criterion": "every requirement in scope tested",
159 "ok": not untested,
160 "value": ", ".join(untested) or "none missing",
161 }
162 )
163 # The version may be tagged only if all four criteria hold.
164 return all(row["ok"] for row in gate_rows)

172 f"{'now' if item['now'] else 'later'}"
173 )
174
175# Evaluate the exit criteria for each day.
176for numbers in SCENARIOS:
177 # Show which day is being checked; the decision is not known yet.
178 gate.update(day=numbers["day"], decision=None)
179 # Evaluate the four criteria.
180 may_tag = check_exit(numbers)
181 # Print the four rows of the check.
182 for row in gate_rows:
183 # One row per criterion: PASS or FAIL, then the measured value.
184 print(
185 f"{numbers['day']:7} {'PASS' if row['ok'] else 'FAIL'} "
186 f"{row['criterion']:36} {row['value']}"
187 )
188 # Store the decision of the day for the picture.
189 gate["decision"] = "tag block7-draft" if may_tag else "do not tag yet"
190 # Keep the decision for the summary.
191 decisions.append((numbers["day"], gate["decision"]))
192 # Print the decision.
193 print(f"{numbers['day']}: {gate['decision']}")
194

196print(
197 "Summary:", "; ".join(f"{day} → {decision}" for day, decision in decisions)
198)

Step-by-step explanation
  1. TYPES is the “who and when” part of the plan: five dictionaries, one per type of testing. Only unit testing runs now; the plan dates the other four.
  2. MIN_BRANCH_COVERAGE is the measurable part of the exit criterion — 80 %, a number anyone can check with a tool.
  3. SCENARIOS holds the team's real numbers on Friday and on Sunday: tests run and passed, branch outcomes executed, open severity-1 defects, requirements in scope and tested.
  4. check_exit() evaluates the four criteria one by one and appends a row for each — all unit tests pass; branch coverage = 16 ÷ 25 = 64 % on Friday, 22 ÷ 25 = 88 % on Sunday; no open severity-1 defect; every requirement in scope tested.
  5. all() returns True only when every row is True: one failed criterion is enough to stop the tag.
  6. Friday: four criteria fail → “do not tag yet”. Sunday, after the corrections: all four hold → “tag block7-draft”.
  7. The picture shows the V-model with the five types (green: running now; grey: dated in the plan) and the four criteria lighting up as they are evaluated.

Five flash-cards — turn each one

verification versus validationclick or press Enter to turn
Verification: are we building the product right? — checks against the specification (reviews; unit, integration and system tests). Validation: are we building the right product? — checks against the users' needs (user acceptance tests, prototypes). Boehm, 1979.
error → defect → failureclick or press Enter to turn
An error is a human mistake (reading “at least 10” as “more than 10”). It can leave a defect in the code (> instead of >=). When the defective line runs with a triggering value, a failure appears: observable wrong behaviour (a cancellation refused at exactly 10 minutes).
the five types of testingclick or press Enter to turn
Unit — one function or class alone. Integration — the interfaces between parts. System — the whole product against the SRS (Software Requirements Specification). User acceptance — real users confirm it supports their tasks. Performance — behaviour under load. The first four are levels; performance is a non-functional type, usually run at system level.
load test versus stress testclick or press Enter to turn
A load test checks behaviour at the expected peak load (200 students opening the weekly report). A stress test goes beyond the expected load until the system fails, to see how it fails and whether it recovers.
test plan, entry and exit criteriaclick or press Enter to turn
A test plan gives the scope, the five types with who and when, tools, entry criteria (conditions to start a test activity) and exit criteria (measurable conditions to finish and release — all unit tests pass, branch coverage ≥ 80 %, no open severity-1 defect), and the defect process.

3Part C0:30–0:36

Lesson 3 — Black-box test design

Part C · 0:30–0:36 · Topic 3, LO3 (Learning Outcome 3)

You will be able to: Design test cases from a specification alone: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables and error guessing.

Testing from the specification only 0:30–0:31Slide 23

Black-box testing, also called specification-based testing, designs test cases from the requirements, use cases and user stories alone — the inputs and the expected outputs — without reading the code. It works at every level, from a unit to the whole system.

Why do we need a technique at all? Because testing every input is impossible. A function with two 32-bit integer inputs has 2 to the power 64 — about 1.8 × 10^19 — input combinations. At one billion tests per second, running all of them would take about 585 years. So we choose a small set of inputs with a high chance of revealing defects.

A test case records an identifier, the input and the preconditions, and the expected result, written before the run; after the run you add the actual result and the status, pass or fail. Today's example: StudyBuddy's booking rule.

Equivalence partitioning 0:31–0:33Slide 24

An equivalence class, or partition, is a set of input values that the specification says the program must treat in the same way. If one value of a class reveals a defect, the other values of that class most probably reveal it too. Equivalence partitioning therefore divides each input into valid and invalid classes and tests one representative value per class.

StudyBuddy's requirement FR-04 (functional requirement 04): “A student can book a study session for a group of 2 to 6 students, at least 2 hours and at most 14 days — 336 hours — before it starts.” The group size has three classes: invalid, 1 or fewer; valid, 2 to 6; invalid, 7 or more. A value that is not a whole number — the text “three”, or 2.5 — forms a fourth, invalid class. The hours ahead have three classes: invalid, fewer than 2 — too soon; valid, 2 to 336; invalid, more than 336 — too far.

Two rules. Every input needs at least one invalid class — beginners test only valid values. And test the invalid classes one at a time, with all the other inputs valid; otherwise the first error message hides the second.

Boundary value analysis 0:33–0:34Slide 25

Defects are frequent at the edges of the classes: > written instead of >=, a loop that stops one step early, a rounding in the wrong direction. Boundary value analysis tests the values on each edge and next to it.

In the two-value form you test each boundary and its nearest neighbour in the adjacent class: for group size 2 to 6, the values 1, 2, 6 and 7. In the three-value form you add the nearest value inside the class: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. For hours ahead: 1, 2, 3, 335, 336, 337. Our schedule's Numbers corner uses the three-value form: for 1 to 50 copies, test 0, 1, 2, 49, 50 and 51.

Lab 07 warns about the most common mistake: boundaries on the wrong side. If the rule says “at least 10”, test 9, 10 and 11 — not 5 and 50.

Decision tables 0:34–0:35Slide 26

When the result depends on a combination of conditions, use a decision table. Its rows list the conditions and the actions; each column is a rule — one combination of condition values and the actions it triggers. With three yes-or-no conditions there are at most 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rules. Columns that lead to the same action, and in which one condition does not matter, merge into one rule with a dash, meaning “either value”.

StudyBuddy checks three conditions: Is the group size valid? Is the time valid? Does the session overlap with another session of the same student? If the size is invalid, the booking is refused with the size message, whatever the other two answers are — one rule. If the size is valid and the time is not, the time message — one rule. If both are valid, the overlap decides: book, or refuse with the overlap message — two rules. Eight combinations became four rules, and each rule becomes at least one test case.

Error guessing 0:35–0:36Slide 27

The last technique uses experience. In error guessing the tester adds test cases for mistakes that programs often contain and that the formal techniques do not produce: an empty field; zero; a negative number; a very large number; text in a number field; spaces before or after a value; the same form submitted twice; February 29; the night the clocks change; a different time zone.

Keep a checklist of such cases in your team, and add a line to it every time a defect surprises you. For StudyBuddy: the text “three” in the group-size field, and the same booking submitted twice within one second.

Real-life example — StudyBuddy

StudyBuddy (Team Lynx) — black-box tests for booking a study session

The task this example doesDerive the equivalence classes and the boundary values of the booking rule, write them as black-box test cases in the Lab 07 sheet format, add the decision table of the booking checks and two error-guessing cases, then run every case against the team's first implementation.
How it relates to this lessonApplies Lesson 3: equivalence partitioning, three-value boundary value analysis, a decision table and error guessing — all from the specification, without reading the code.

StudyBuddy helps students find study partners and book sessions. Requirement FR-04 (functional requirement 04) of Team Lynx: “A student can book a study session for a group of 2 to 6 students, at least 2 hours and at most 14 days (336 hours) before it starts. A session may not overlap with another session of the same student.”

Nadia and Omar, the testers of the week, design the cases before they look at Jonas's code. Running them finds one failure, exactly on a boundary. All names and data are fictional.

Step by step
  1. Partition each input (Lesson 3): group size → 1 or fewer, 2–6, 7 or more, not a whole number; hours ahead → fewer than 2, 2–336, more than 336.
  2. Add the three-value boundaries: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 for the group; 1, 2, 3, 335, 336, 337 for the hours. Vary one input at a time and keep the other one typical (4 students, 48 hours).
  3. Build the decision table: 3 conditions, 8 combinations, 4 rules; the overlap rule needs one new case, BB-14 (black-box test case 14).
  4. Add error guessing: the text “three” (BB-15 (black-box test case 15)) and a double submission (BB-16 (black-box test case 16), run by hand at system level).
  5. Write every expected result before running anything — in the Lab 07 sheet format.
  6. Run the cases. 14 of 15 automatic cases pass. BB-08 (black-box test case 08) fails: a booking exactly 2 hours ahead is refused. The code checks hours_ahead > 2; the requirement says “at least 2”. One character, > instead of >=, found exactly on the boundary.

Demo 3 — black-box tests for StudyBuddy bookings · Python, 495 recorded steps

The task this program does: Derives the three-value boundary values of FR-04 (functional requirement 04) for the group size and the hours ahead, adds the typical case, the overlap rule of the decision table and an error-guessing case, writes the expected result of every case from the specification, then runs the 15 cases against Jonas's can_book().

How it relates to the lecture: Lesson 3: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, a decision table and error guessing; the printed rows have the columns of the Lab 07 black-box sheet.

1# =============================================================================
2# CS 330 · Class 7 · Lesson 3 — Demo 3: black-box tests for StudyBuddy bookings
3# TASK: derive the three-value boundary values of FR-04 (functional requirement
4# 04) for the group size (2 to 6) and the hours ahead (2 to 336), add the
5# typical case, the overlap rule of the decision table and one error-guessing
6# case, write the expected result of every case from the specification, then
7# run all 15 cases against Jonas's first implementation of can_book().
8# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 3 — equivalence partitioning, boundary value
9# analysis, decision tables and error guessing; the table it prints has the
10# columns of the Lab 07 black-box sheet.
11# Fictional people and data only (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, section 6.7).
12# Runs with Python 3.10 or newer and needs no extra package.
13# =============================================================================
14
15# FR-04 (functional requirement 04): a group has 2 to 6 students.
16MIN_GROUP, MAX_GROUP = 2, 6
17# FR-04 (functional requirement 04): a session is booked at least 2 hours and
18# at most 14 days (336 hours) ahead.
19MIN_HOURS, MAX_HOURS = 2, 336
20# The typical values used for the input that is not being varied.
21TYPICAL_GROUP, TYPICAL_HOURS = 4, 48
22
23# Every test case of the run; the picture on the right reads this list.
24cases = []
25# The case being executed now (None before the run starts).
26current = None
27
28
29# boundary_values() returns the three-value boundaries of a valid range:
30# outside, on and inside each edge.
31def boundary_values(low, high):
32 # For 2–6 this gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7; for 2–336 it gives 1, 2, 3, 335,
33 # 336, 337.
34 return [low - 1, low, low + 1, high - 1, high, high + 1]
35
36
37# expected_from_spec() is the testers' partition table of FR-04 (functional
38# requirement 04): it states what MUST happen, from the specification.
39def expected_from_spec(group, hours, overlaps):
40 # A group size that is not a whole number, or outside 2–6, is an invalid
41 # class: refused with the size message.
42 if not isinstance(group, int) or group < MIN_GROUP or group > MAX_GROUP:
43 # The expected result for the invalid size classes.
44 return "refused — size"
45 # Hours outside 2–336 are an invalid class: refused with the time message.
46 if hours < MIN_HOURS or hours > MAX_HOURS:
47 # The expected result for the invalid time classes.
48 return "refused — time"
49 # Decision-table rule 3: an overlap with another session of the student is
50 # refused.
51 if overlaps:
52 # The expected result for the overlap rule.
53 return "refused — overlap"
54 # Every other combination is valid: the session is booked.
55 return "booked"
56
57
58# can_book() is Jonas's first implementation — the code under test.
59def can_book(group_size, hours_ahead, overlaps):
60 # The size check: whole number from 2 to 6.
61 if not isinstance(group_size, int) or group_size < 2 or group_size > 6:
62 # Refuse with the size message.
63 return "refused — size"
64 # The time check — the defect is here: "> 2" refuses exactly 2 hours, but
65 # FR-04 (functional requirement 04) says "at least 2".
66 time_ok = hours_ahead > 2 and hours_ahead <= 336
67 # If the time is not acceptable, refuse with the time message.
68 if not time_ok:
69 # Refuse with the time message.
70 return "refused — time"
71 # The overlap check.
72 if overlaps:
73 # Refuse with the overlap message.
74 return "refused — overlap"
75 # All checks passed.
76 return "booked"
77
78
79# add_case() creates one test case with its identifier, inputs, technique and
80# expected result.
81def add_case(group, hours, overlaps, technique):
82 # Identifiers follow the Lab 07 sheet: BB-01 (black-box test case 01),
83 # BB-02 (black-box test case 02), ...
84 case_id = f"BB-{len(cases) + 1:02d}"
85 # The expected result is written BEFORE the run, from the specification
86 # only.
87 expected = expected_from_spec(group, hours, overlaps)
88 # Store the case; "actual" and "status" stay empty until the run.
89 cases.append(
90 {
91 "id": case_id,
92 "group": group,
93 "hours": hours,
94 "overlaps": overlaps,
95 "technique": technique,
96 # The two result fields are filled in during the run.
97 "expected": expected,
98 "actual": None,
99 "status": None,
100 }
101 )
102
103
104# Group size: the six boundary values, with the hours kept typical.
105for group in boundary_values(MIN_GROUP, MAX_GROUP):
106 # One case per boundary value of the group size.
107 add_case(group, TYPICAL_HOURS, False, "boundary: group size")
108# Hours ahead: the six boundary values, with the group size kept typical.
109for hours in boundary_values(MIN_HOURS, MAX_HOURS):
110 # One case per boundary value of the hours.
111 add_case(TYPICAL_GROUP, hours, False, "boundary: hours ahead")
112# The typical case: both inputs valid and far from the edges.
113add_case(TYPICAL_GROUP, TYPICAL_HOURS, False, "typical value")
114# Decision-table rule 3: everything valid, but the session overlaps another
115# one.
116add_case(TYPICAL_GROUP, TYPICAL_HOURS, True, "decision table: overlap")
117# Error guessing: text typed into the group-size field.
118add_case("three", TYPICAL_HOURS, False, "error guessing: text")
119# Print how many cases were designed before running anything.
120print(f"{len(cases)} cases designed from FR-04 before running the code")
121
122# Run every case against the implementation.
123for case in cases:
124 # Point the picture at the case being executed.
125 current = case["id"]
126 # Call the code under test with the inputs of the case.
127 case["actual"] = can_book(case["group"], case["hours"], case["overlaps"])
128 # A case passes when the actual result equals the expected result.
129 case["status"] = "pass" if case["actual"] == case["expected"] else "FAIL"
130 # Print the case as one row of the black-box sheet.
131 print(
132 f"{case['id']} group={case['group']!s:6} hours={case['hours']:<4} "
133 f"{case['expected']:18} {case['actual']:18} {case['status']}"
134 )
135
136# The run is over: nothing is being executed any more.
137current = None
138# Collect the failing cases.
139failures = [case["id"] for case in cases if case["status"] == "FAIL"]
140# Print the summary: how many passed, which failed.
141print(
142 f"{len(cases) - len(failures)} of {len(cases)} pass; "
143 f"failing: {', '.join(failures) or 'none'}"
144)
Execution trace — every step, click one to inspect it
Variables at this step
Output
Step-by-step explanation
  1. The three constant lines hold the six numbers of FR-04 (functional requirement 04): group size 2 to 6, hours ahead 2 to 336, and the typical values (4 students, 48 hours) used for the input that is kept fixed.
  2. boundary_values(2, 6) returns 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 — outside, on and inside each edge; boundary_values(2, 336) returns 1, 2, 3, 335, 336, 337.
  3. expected_from_spec() is the testers' partition table: it says what must happen for each class, from the requirement only. It never looks at Jonas's code.
  4. can_book() is the code under test. Its time check is hours_ahead > 2 — the defect the run will find.
  5. add_case() builds the 15 cases: six group-size boundaries, six hour boundaries, the typical case, the overlap rule and the text “three”. Every expected result is fixed before anything runs.
  6. The run calls can_book() for each case and compares actual with expected. Watch the dots on the two number lines turn green — and one turn red.
  7. BB-08 (black-box test case 08) fails: 2 hours ahead is refused, although “at least 2” allows it. One character, > instead of >=, found exactly on the boundary — the reason boundary value analysis exists.

Five flash-cards — turn each one

black-box testingclick or press Enter to turn
Designing test cases from the specification alone — requirements, use cases, user stories — with inputs and expected outputs, without reading the code. It is used at every level of testing.
equivalence partitioningclick or press Enter to turn
Divide each input into classes that the specification treats the same way — valid and invalid — and test one representative value per class. Group size 2–6: 1 or fewer (invalid), 2 to 6 (valid), 7 or more (invalid), not a whole number (invalid).
boundary value analysisclick or press Enter to turn
Test on each edge of a class and next to it, because comparison defects (> instead of >=) show there. Three-value for 2–6: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. Two-value: 1, 2, 6, 7. For 1–50 copies: 0, 1, 2, 49, 50, 51.
decision tableclick or press Enter to turn
Conditions and actions in rows; one column, called a rule, per combination of condition values. With 3 yes-or-no conditions there are at most 8 rules; rules with the same action where a condition does not matter merge (–). Each rule gives at least one test case.
error guessingclick or press Enter to turn
Experience-based test cases for typical mistakes that formal techniques miss: empty input, zero, negative and very large values, text in a number field, double submission, February 29, clock changes and time zones.

4Part C0:36–0:41

Lesson 4 — White-box test design: coverage, flow graphs and cyclomatic complexity

Part C · 0:36–0:41 · Topic 3, LO3 (Learning Outcome 3)

You will be able to: Measure statement and branch coverage, draw the flow graph of a function, compute V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) in three ways, and design one test per basis path.

Testing from the code: coverage 0:36–0:37Slide 31

White-box testing, also called structure-based or glass-box testing, designs test cases from the internal structure of the code, so that chosen parts of it — statements, branches, paths — are executed. It complements black-box testing: it finds code that no specification-based test reaches.

Code coverage is the percentage of a structural element that a test suite executes. Statement coverage is the number of statements executed divided by the number of statements: 34 of 40 gives 85 %. Branch coverage, also called decision coverage, is the number of decision outcomes executed divided by the number of outcomes; every if has two outcomes, true and false.

100 % branch coverage implies 100 % statement coverage, but not the reverse. Take if x > 0: y = 1 and the single test x = 5: every statement runs — 100 % statement coverage — but only the true outcome is taken: 50 % branch coverage. And remember what Lab 07 says: coverage shows what was not tested; it cannot show that a test checks the right result. A test without an assertion raises coverage and proves nothing.

The flow graph 0:37–0:38Slide 32

A flow graph represents the control flow of one function. Each node is a block of statements or a single decision; each edge is a possible transfer of control from one node to the next. A decision node has two outgoing edges, yes and no.

One rule matters for exams and for Lab 07: a compound condition such as exit_blocked and after_hours is split into one node per simple condition, because Python evaluates the second part only when the first is true — the program can leave after the first part. Today's function, SafeCampus's triage_level(), gives a graph of 9 nodes and 12 edges.

Cyclomatic complexity — three ways to compute it 0:38–0:40Slide 33

In 1976 Thomas McCabe defined the cyclomatic complexity of a flow graph G, written V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) (Thomas McCabe, “A Complexity Measure”, 1976 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers digital library)↗). It can be computed in three ways, and the three must agree. First, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = E − N + 2, where E is the number of edges and N the number of nodes of one connected graph: for triage_level(), 12 − 9 + 2 = 5. Second, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = the number of simple decisions + 1: four decisions — injury, exit blocked, after hours, reports today — plus one gives 5. Third, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = the number of regions of the drawn graph, counting the outside: 5.

What does the number mean? V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) is the number of linearly independent paths through the function — a basis path set: every other path is a combination of these. It is the number of tests that basis path testing requires, and an upper limit for the number of tests needed for full branch coverage. It is also a complexity measure: McCabe proposed 10 as an upper limit for one module, and the NIST SP 500-235 (National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 500-235)↗ report on structured testing discusses this limit. A function above it is a candidate for splitting.

Basis path testing 0:40–0:41Slide 34

Basis path testing turns the number into tests, in five steps: draw the flow graph; compute V(G) (cyclomatic complexity); choose V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) independent paths; for each path, choose inputs that force it and write the expected result; run the tests and measure coverage.

To choose the paths, McCabe's baseline method is simple: start with the most common path, then flip one decision at a time. For triage_level() the baseline is the everyday report — nobody injured, exit clear, few reports — which gives “normal”. Flipping the four decisions gives four more paths: injured gives “urgent”; exit blocked in the daytime gives “normal”; exit blocked after hours gives “high”; three reports today give “high”. Five paths, five tests. The function has six complete paths, but the sixth is a combination of the five.

Team Heron's first two tests reached 71.4 % statement coverage and 66.7 % branch coverage; the five basis-path tests reach 100 % of both. Your coverage tool measures this for you — coverage.py↗ with the branch option for Python, JaCoCo↗ for Java, Jest↗ for JavaScript. Expect the tool to show a different number from a count by hand: coverage.py counts the whole file — the def line and the constant are statements too — and with the branch option it prints one combined figure, (statements run + branch outcomes taken) ÷ (statements + outcomes). For Team Heron's two tests that is (7 + 4) ÷ (9 + 6) = 73 %. Both numbers are correct; they count different things.

Real-life example — SafeCampus

SafeCampus (Team Heron) — white-box tests for the triage rule

The task this example doesDraw the flow graph of triage_level(), compute V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) in three ways, choose the basis paths with the baseline method, write one test per path with its expected result, and measure statement and branch coverage before and after.
How it relates to this lessonApplies Lesson 4: flow graph with a split compound condition, cyclomatic complexity, basis path testing, statement and branch coverage.

SafeCampus lets students report hazards on campus. Requirement FR-07 (functional requirement 07) of Team Heron: “The system shall give each hazard report a triage level: urgent if someone is injured; high if an emergency exit is blocked outside opening hours, or if 3 or more reports about the same place arrived today; normal otherwise.”

Priya wrote the function test-first for the urgent case and for the everyday case. Before tagging, Malik measures the coverage and finds that two statements never ran. All names and data are fictional.

REPEAT_LIMIT = 3


def triage_level(injury, exit_blocked, after_hours, reports_today):
    """Return the triage level of one hazard report (FR-07)."""
    if injury:
        return "urgent"
    if exit_blocked and after_hours:
        return "high"
    if reports_today >= REPEAT_LIMIT:
        return "high"
    return "normal"
Step by step
  1. Number the nodes of the code: 9 nodes, because exit_blocked and after_hours becomes two decision nodes (3 and 4).
  2. Draw the edges: 12 edges — two from each of the four decisions, and one from each of the four return blocks to the end node.
  3. Compute V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) three ways: 12 − 9 + 2 = 5; 4 decisions + 1 = 5; 5 regions in Figure 4. They agree.
  4. Choose the basis paths by the baseline method: the everyday path 1-3-6-8-9, then flip node 1, node 3, node 4 and node 6 — five paths.
  5. Write one test per path with its inputs and expected result (UT-01 (unit test 01) to UT-05 (unit test 05)); the expected results come from FR-07 (functional requirement 07), not from the code.
  6. Measure coverage. Priya's first two tests (paths 1 and 2): 5 of 7 statements = 71.4 %, 4 of 6 decision outcomes = 66.7 %; both return "high" lines never ran. With the five basis-path tests: 7 of 7 and 6 of 6 — 100 %.
  7. Notice the difference between the two measures: four tests (paths 1, 2, 4 and 5) already give 100 % branch coverage on the source lines; path 3 — exit blocked in the daytime — is required only because the compound condition was split. Basis path testing checks more than branch coverage.

Demo 4 — basis paths and coverage of triage_level() · Python, 705 recorded steps

The task this program does: Describes the flow graph of triage_level() as data, computes V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) with two formulas, checks that the five basis paths of the baseline method are independent and use all twelve edges, runs the tests, and measures statement and branch coverage for the team's two tests and for the five basis-path tests.

How it relates to the lecture: Lesson 4: flow graph with a split compound condition, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = E − N + 2 = decisions + 1, basis path testing and the two coverage measures — Lab 07, Step 4.

1# =============================================================================
2# CS 330 · Class 7 · Lesson 4 — Demo 4: basis paths and coverage of
3# triage_level()
4# TASK: describe the flow graph of SafeCampus's triage_level() as data, compute
5# V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) with two formulas, check that the five basis
6# paths
7# of the baseline method are independent, run the tests, and measure
8# statement
9# and branch coverage — first for the team's two tests, then for the five
10# basis-path tests.
11# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 4 — flow graph, compound condition split into
12# two nodes, V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = E − N + 2 = decisions + 1, basis
13# path testing, statement
14# and branch coverage; the same work is Lab 07, Step 4.
15# Fictional people and data only (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, section 6.7).
16# Runs with Python 3.10 or newer and needs no extra package.
17# =============================================================================
18
19# FR-07 (functional requirement 07): three or more reports about the same place
20# today raise the level to "high".
21REPEAT_LIMIT = 3
22
23
24# triage_level() is the code under test, exactly as Team Heron wrote it.
25def triage_level(injury, exit_blocked, after_hours, reports_today):
26 # The docstring states what the function returns and which requirement it
27 # implements.
28 """Return the triage level of one hazard report (FR-07)."""
29 # Decision 1 (node 1): someone is injured.
30 if injury:
31 # Node 2: the most serious level.
32 return "urgent"
33 # Decisions 2 and 3 (nodes 3 and 4): the exit is blocked AND it is outside
34 # opening hours.
35 if exit_blocked and after_hours:
36 # Node 5.
37 return "high"
38 # Decision 4 (node 6): repeated reports about the same place.
39 if reports_today >= REPEAT_LIMIT:
40 # Node 7.
41 return "high"
42 # Node 8: everything else.
43 return "normal"
44
45
46# The nodes of the flow graph: number → what the node does.
47NODES = {
48 1: "injury?",
49 2: 'return "urgent"',
50 3: "exit_blocked?",
51 4: "after_hours?",
52 5: 'return "high"',
53 # Nodes 6 to 9: the third if, its two returns, and the common end node.
54 6: "reports_today >= 3?",
55 7: 'return "high"',
56 8: 'return "normal"',
57 9: "end",
58}
59# The edges: (from node, to node, label). Each decision has a "yes" and a "no"
60# edge.
61EDGES = [
62 (1, 2, "yes"),
63 (1, 3, "no"),
64 (2, 9, ""),
65 (3, 4, "yes"),
66 (3, 6, "no"),
67 (4, 5, "yes"),
68 # The remaining edges: the "no" of node 4, the returns into the end node,
69 # and node 6.
70 (4, 6, "no"),
71 (5, 9, ""),
72 (6, 7, "yes"),
73 (6, 8, "no"),
74 (7, 9, ""),
75 (8, 9, ""),
76]
77# The decision nodes (one simple condition each).
78DECISIONS = [1, 3, 4, 6]
79# Which source statement each node belongs to: nodes 3 and 4 are the same line
80# of code.
81STATEMENT_OF_NODE = {
82 1: "if injury",
83 2: 'return "urgent"',
84 3: "if exit_blocked and after_hours",
85 # Node 4 is the second half of the same if statement.
86 4: "if exit_blocked and after_hours",
87 5: 'return "high" (exit)',
88 6: "if reports_today >= 3",
89 # Nodes 7 and 8 are the last two return statements.
90 7: 'return "high" (repeats)',
91 8: 'return "normal"',
92}
93# The seven statements of the function body.
94STATEMENTS = sorted(set(STATEMENT_OF_NODE.values()))
95# Which decision outcome, at the level of the source line, each edge produces.
96OUTCOME_OF_EDGE = {
97 (1, 2): "if injury: true",
98 (1, 3): "if injury: false",
99 # The second if is true only through edge 4→5; it is false through 3→6 or
100 # 4→6.
101 (4, 5): "if exit_blocked and after_hours: true",
102 (3, 6): "if exit_blocked and after_hours: false",
103 # Edge 4→6 also gives the false outcome of the second if.
104 (4, 6): "if exit_blocked and after_hours: false",
105 # The third if: true through 6→7, false through 6→8.
106 (6, 7): "if reports_today >= 3: true",
107 (6, 8): "if reports_today >= 3: false",
108}
109# The six decision outcomes of the source code (three ifs × true/false).
110OUTCOMES = sorted(set(OUTCOME_OF_EDGE.values()))
111
112# Three computations of V(G) (cyclomatic complexity); the picture shows them.
113vg = {}
114# The path being walked now, and everything covered so far by the current test
115# set.
116current_path = []
117# The nodes and edges covered so far by the current test set.
118covered_nodes, covered_edges = set(), set()
119# The coverage figures of each test set.
120coverage = {}
121# Which test set is running: "two tests" or "basis paths".
122test_set = None
123
124
125# condition_holds() evaluates the simple condition of one decision node for the
126# given inputs.
127def condition_holds(node, inputs):
128 # Node 1 asks whether someone is injured.
129 if node == 1:
130 # The answer comes straight from the input.
131 return inputs["injury"]
132 # Node 3 asks whether the exit is blocked.
133 if node == 3:
134 # The answer comes straight from the input.
135 return inputs["exit_blocked"]
136 # Node 4 asks whether it is outside opening hours.
137 if node == 4:
138 # The answer comes straight from the input.
139 return inputs["after_hours"]
140 # Node 6 asks whether there were 3 or more reports today.
141 return inputs["reports_today"] >= REPEAT_LIMIT
142
143
144# NEXT tells, for each node, where each label leads: NEXT[1]["yes"] is 2,
145# NEXT[2][""] is 9.
146NEXT = {}
147# Fill NEXT from the list of edges, one edge at a time.
148for start, end, label in EDGES:
149 # Create the entry of the start node if needed, then store where this label
150 # leads.
151 NEXT.setdefault(start, {})[label] = end
152
153
154# walk() follows the flow graph from node 1 to the end node for one set of
155# inputs and returns the path.
156def walk(inputs):
157 # Every path starts at node 1.
158 path = [1]
159 # Continue until the end node (9) is reached.
160 while path[-1] != 9:
161 # A decision node answers "yes" or "no"; a block node has a single,
162 # unlabelled edge.
163 if path[-1] in DECISIONS:
164 # Evaluate the simple condition of this decision node.
165 label = "yes" if condition_holds(path[-1], inputs) else "no"
166 # Otherwise the node is a block: follow its only edge.
167 else:
168 # The single edge of a block node has an empty label.
169 label = ""
170 # Append the node that this label leads to.
171 path.append(NEXT[path[-1]][label])
172 # The complete path from start to end.
173 return path
174
175
176# Computation 1: V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = E − N + 2 (edges − nodes + 2
177# for one connected graph).
178vg["E − N + 2"] = len(EDGES) - len(NODES) + 2
179# Computation 2: V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = number of simple decisions + 1.
180vg["decisions + 1"] = len(DECISIONS) + 1
181# Print the two computations.
182print(
183 f"E = {len(EDGES)}, N = {len(NODES)}: V(G) = {vg['E − N + 2']}; "
184 f"decisions + 1 = {vg['decisions + 1']}"
185)
186
187# The baseline method: the everyday path first, then flip one decision at a
188# time (nodes 1, 3, 4, 6).
189BASIS = [
190 (
191 "baseline",
192 dict(
193 injury=False,
194 exit_blocked=False,
195 after_hours=False,
196 reports_today=0,
197 ),
198 "normal",
199 ),
200 # Flip node 1: someone is injured.
201 (
202 "flip node 1",
203 dict(
204 injury=True, exit_blocked=False, after_hours=False, reports_today=0
205 ),
206 "urgent",
207 ),
208 # Flip node 3: the exit is blocked, but it is daytime.
209 (
210 "flip node 3",
211 dict(
212 injury=False, exit_blocked=True, after_hours=False, reports_today=0
213 ),
214 "normal",
215 ),
216 # Flip node 4: the exit is blocked and it is after hours.
217 (
218 "flip node 4",
219 dict(
220 injury=False, exit_blocked=True, after_hours=True, reports_today=0
221 ),
222 "high",
223 ),
224 # Flip node 6: the exit is clear, but three reports arrived today.
225 (
226 "flip node 6",
227 dict(
228 injury=False,
229 exit_blocked=False,
230 after_hours=False,
231 reports_today=3,
232 ),
233 "high",
234 ),
235]
236
237# A check, not a formula: count the paths that are independent — each one must
238# use at least one edge not used before.
239edges_seen = set()
240# The number of independent paths found so far.
241independent = 0
242# Walk the five basis inputs.
243for name, inputs, expected in BASIS:
244 # The path these inputs force through the graph.
245 current_path = walk(inputs)
246 # The edges of this path, as (from, to) pairs.
247 path_edges = set(zip(current_path, current_path[1:]))
248 # A path is independent of the earlier ones if it adds at least one new
249 # edge.
250 if path_edges - edges_seen:
251 # Count it.
252 independent += 1
253 # Remember all edges seen so far.
254 edges_seen |= path_edges
255 # Print the path with its node numbers.
256 print(f"{name:12} path {'-'.join(map(str, current_path))}")
257# The number of independent basis paths must equal V(G) (cyclomatic
258# complexity).
259vg["independent paths"] = independent
260# Print it, and check that every edge of the graph was used.
261print(
262 f"independent paths = {independent}; all {len(EDGES)} edges used: "
263 f"{edges_seen == {(a, b) for a, b, _ in EDGES}}"
264)
265
266
267# run_tests() runs a set of tests, checks each result, and measures statement
268# and branch coverage.
269def run_tests(label, tests):
270 # Name the set, so that the picture can show it.
271 global test_set
272 # The test set now running.
273 test_set = label
274 # Start with nothing covered.
275 covered_nodes.clear()
276 # Clear the covered edges too.
277 covered_edges.clear()
278 # Run each test of the set.
279 for name, inputs, expected in tests:
280 # The real function gives the actual result — this is the test itself.
281 actual = triage_level(**inputs)
282 # The path through the flow graph shows which statements and outcomes
283 # were executed.
284 path = walk(inputs)
285 # Mark the nodes of the path as covered.
286 covered_nodes.update(path)
287 # Mark its edges as covered.
288 covered_edges.update(zip(path, path[1:]))
289 # Print the test: expected, actual, pass or fail.
290 print(
291 f" {name:12} expected {expected:7} actual {actual:7} "
292 f"{'pass' if actual == expected else 'FAIL'}"
293 )
294 # The statements executed: the statements of the covered nodes.
295 executed = {
296 STATEMENT_OF_NODE[node]
297 for node in covered_nodes
298 if node in STATEMENT_OF_NODE
299 }
300 # The decision outcomes executed: the outcomes of the covered edges.
301 outcomes = {
302 OUTCOME_OF_EDGE[edge]
303 for edge in covered_edges
304 if edge in OUTCOME_OF_EDGE
305 }
306 # Statement coverage = executed statements ÷ statements × 100.
307 statement = 100 * len(executed) / len(STATEMENTS)
308 # Branch coverage = executed outcomes ÷ outcomes × 100.
309 branch = 100 * len(outcomes) / len(OUTCOMES)
310 # Store the figures for the picture.
311 coverage[label] = {
312 "statement": round(statement, 1),
313 "branch": round(branch, 1),
314 "missing": sorted(set(STATEMENTS) - executed),
315 }
316 # Print the two coverage figures.
317 print(
318 f"{label}: statements {len(executed)}/{len(STATEMENTS)} = "
319 f"{statement:.1f} %, branches {len(outcomes)}/{len(OUTCOMES)} = "
320 f"{branch:.1f} %"
321 )
322
323
324# The team's first two tests: someone injured, and the everyday report.
325run_tests("two tests", [BASIS[1], BASIS[0]])
326# The five basis-path tests.
327run_tests("basis paths", BASIS)
