Step-by-step explanation
  1. triage_level() is the code under test: four simple decisions, because exit_blocked and after_hours is two decisions.
  2. NODES and EDGES describe the flow graph: 9 nodes and 12 edges, each decision with a “yes” and a “no” edge. NEXT turns the edge list into a table: from this node, with this answer, go there.
  3. STATEMENT_OF_NODE and OUTCOME_OF_EDGE link the graph back to the source code: nodes 3 and 4 belong to the same if line, which coverage tools count as one decision with two outcomes.
  4. walk() follows the graph for one set of inputs — the same decisions the function makes — and returns the path, such as 1-3-6-8-9.
  5. V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) with two formulas: 12 − 9 + 2 = 5 and 4 decisions + 1 = 5 (the third, five regions, is counted on Figure 4). Then a check: five basis paths, each adding at least one edge not used before — exactly as many independent paths as V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) says — and all twelve edges used.
  6. run_tests() calls the real function for each test, compares actual and expected, and marks the nodes and edges of its path as covered.
  7. The team's two tests reach 5 of 7 statements (71.4 %) and 4 of 6 outcomes (66.7 %); the five basis-path tests reach 100 % of both. Watch the graph fill in.

white-box testingclick or press Enter to turn
Designing test cases from the internal structure of the code, so that chosen statements, branches or paths are executed. Also called structure-based or glass-box testing; it complements black-box testing.
statement coverageclick or press Enter to turn
Statements executed ÷ all statements × 100. 34 of 40 → 85 %. It shows which code never ran; it does not show whether the tests checked the right results.
branch coverageclick or press Enter to turn
Decision outcomes executed ÷ all outcomes × 100 — every if has a true and a false outcome. 100 % branch coverage implies 100 % statement coverage, but not the reverse (if x > 0: y = 1 with x = 5: 100 % statements, 50 % branches).
flow graphclick or press Enter to turn
A drawing of one function's control flow: nodes are blocks of statements or single decisions, edges are possible transfers of control. A compound condition a and b becomes two decision nodes.
V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) and basis pathsclick or press Enter to turn
V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) = E − N + 2 = simple decisions + 1 = regions (McCabe, 1976). It is the number of linearly independent paths — the basis path set — so basis path testing needs V(G) (cyclomatic complexity) tests. triage_level(): 12 − 9 + 2 = 5.

5Part D0:45–0:56

Lesson 5 — Test-Driven Development, test doubles, debugging and defects

Part D · 0:45–0:56 · Topic 3, LO3 (Learning Outcome 3)

You will be able to: Write code test-first in red–green–refactor cycles, use a unit-test framework, replace dependencies with stubs and mocks, debug systematically, and report defects with severity, priority and defect density.

Test-Driven Development: red, green, refactor 0:45–0:48Slide 40

Test-Driven Development, TDD (Test-Driven Development), is a way of writing code in very short cycles in which the test is written before the code. Kent Beck described it in 2002 in Test-Driven Development: By Example (the publisher's page↗); it is one of the XP (Extreme Programming) practices you met in Class 4.

Each cycle has three steps. Red: write one small test for the next piece of behaviour and run it. It fails — the test runner shows it in red. The failure proves two things: the behaviour is not there yet, and the test is able to fail. A test that has never failed may be checking nothing. Green: write the simplest code that makes this test, and all the earlier ones, pass. Nothing more. Refactor: improve the code — names, constants, duplication — while every test stays green. Then the next cycle.

Take QueueLess's reminder rule, FR-09 (functional requirement 09): the student receives one reminder when 5 minutes or less remain before the pick-up slot, and none once the slot has started. Red: a test says that 5 minutes left means “remind”; it fails, because the function has no body yet — it only raises NotImplementedError. Green: return minutes_left <= 5. Next cycle, red again: a test says that −1 minute — the slot has started — means “no reminder”; it fails, because −1 is less than 5. Green: return 0 <= minutes_left <= 5. Refactor: the 5 becomes the named constant REMINDER_MINUTES. Each step takes a few minutes.

What are the benefits? Every requirement becomes an executable check; the code stays testable, because it was written to be tested; and the growing suite is re-run at every change, which is regression testing at no extra cost. The cost is more code to maintain — tests must be as readable as the product code.

Unit-test frameworks and the shape of a test 0:48–0:50Slide 41

You do not run tests by hand. A unit-test framework finds the test functions, runs them, compares actual and expected results through assertions, prepares shared test data through fixtures, and reports which tests passed and which failed, with the reason. The family is called xUnit — the x stands for the language: it began with Kent Beck's SUnit for Smalltalk, and JUnit, written by Kent Beck and Erich Gamma for Java in 1997, made it widespread: JUnit↗ for Java, pytest↗ for Python, Jest↗ for JavaScript. Lab 07 gives you a starter for each of the three.

Every unit test has the same shape, called Arrange–Act–Assert: arrange the data, act by calling the unit once, assert the expected result. One behaviour per test, and a name that states the behaviour — test_no_reminder_after_slot_started, not test3 — so that the report of a failed test reads like a sentence.

Two more rules from Lab 07. Each test prepares its own data and never depends on another test. And never let a test depend on today's date or the real clock: pass the time in as a parameter, or replace the clock — which brings us to test doubles.

Stubs, mocks and fakes 0:50–0:52Slide 42

Most units call other units: the clock, the database, the notification service, a payment service. In a unit test we replace them with test doubles — objects that take the place of a real component during a test. Gerard Meszaros named the kinds in 2007; Martin Fowler explains the difference in his article Mocks Aren't Stubs↗.

A stub returns answers prepared by the test: a clock that always says 11:55. It controls the inputs that the unit receives. A mock records the calls that the unit makes, so that the test can check them afterwards: the notifier must be called exactly once, for order 42. It checks the outputs that the unit sends. Strictly, a double that records calls for later checking is called a spy; in everyday use, and in Python's unittest.mock↗ library, both are called mocks. A fake is a simplified but working implementation — an in-memory list instead of the database.

Doubles also serve integration testing: top-down integration replaces lower modules that are not ready with stubs, and bottom-up integration calls the modules under test with drivers. One warning: a unit test that replaces every neighbour proves only that the unit talks correctly to the doubles. The real connections still need integration tests — they come in Lab 08.

Debugging: from failure to corrected defect 0:52–0:54Slide 43

Testing reveals a failure; debugging is the work of locating and correcting the defect that causes it. Do it as a sequence of steps, not by changing code at random.

One: reproduce the failure reliably, with the smallest input that still shows it. Two: write a test that fails because of it — in the TDD (Test-Driven Development) style, red first. Three: locate the defect by forming a hypothesis and checking it — read the code, print or log values, or set a breakpoint in the debugger of your editor, stop the program at that line and inspect the variables step by step. When a failure appeared between two versions, git bisect↗ performs a binary search over the commits and finds the commit that introduced it. Four: correct the cause, not the symptom. Five: run the new test and then the whole suite. Six: record the defect, so that its history is not lost.

Defect reports, severity, priority and defect density 0:54–0:56Slide 44

A defect report — a bug report — must let another person reproduce the failure without asking you anything. It contains an identifier; a one-line title that says what fails and where; the steps to reproduce; the expected result and the actual result; the version and the environment; the severity; the priority; the status; and evidence such as a screenshot or a log. In your repository a defect report is a GitHub issue↗ with the labels bug, severity and priority.

Severity and priority are different. Severity is how serious the effect of the defect is on the product and its users — 1 critical, 2 major, 3 minor. Priority is how soon it must be corrected — high, medium, low — a decision of the team and the client. A spelling mistake in the title of the home page: low severity, high priority, because every user sees it. A crash in an export function that no one uses yet: high severity, lower priority. A report also has a life cycle: new, assigned, corrected, verified, closed — or reopened.

Finally, the number. Defect density is the number of defects divided by the size of the code in KLOC (thousands of lines of code): 12 defects in 3,000 lines give 4 defects per thousand lines. Use it to compare versions and modules of your own product — never people.

Real-life example — QueueLess

QueueLess (Team Falcon) — test-first: the pick-up reminder, with a stub clock and a mock notifier

The task this example doesImplement the reminder rule test-first in red–green–refactor cycles; then test the reminder sender in isolation with a stub clock and a mock notifier. The mock exposes a defect — a duplicate reminder — which becomes a defect report with severity and priority, and the team updates its defect density.
How it relates to this lessonApplies Lesson 5: the TDD (Test-Driven Development) cycle, a unit-test framework's shape (Arrange–Act–Assert), test doubles, debugging, the defect report, severity versus priority, defect density.

QueueLess lets students pre-order lunch and pick it up in a time slot. It is the worked example of the Lab 07 template, which already records defects #11 and #12 in 420 lines of code. In Sprint 1 Team Falcon adds requirement FR-09 (functional requirement 09): “The system shall send the student one reminder when 5 minutes or less remain before the pick-up slot starts, and no reminder once the slot has started.”

Ines and Kwame work as a pair; the times are minutes after midnight, so 11:55 is 715 and 12:00 is 720. All names and data are fictional.

Step by step
  1. Red. UT-11 (unit test 11) says that 5 minutes left means “remind”. It fails — the function only raises “not implemented”. Commit: “Add failing test for reminder at 5 minutes (FR-09 (functional requirement 09))”.
  2. Green. return minutes_left <= 5. UT-11 (unit test 11) passes. UT-12 (unit test 12) (6 minutes → no reminder) passes at once — a boundary that is already right, kept as documentation.
  3. Red again. UT-13 (unit test 13) says that −1 minute — the slot has started — means “no reminder”. It fails: −1 is less than 5.
  4. Green. return 0 <= minutes_left <= 5. All tests pass; UT-14 (unit test 14) (0 minutes → remind) is added and passes.
  5. Refactor. The 5 becomes REMINDER_MINUTES = 5; all four tests stay green. Commit: “Name the reminder limit (FR-09 (functional requirement 09))”.
  6. Stub and mock. send_due_reminders(orders, clock, notifier) gets a stub clock fixed at 11:55 and a mock notifier. UT-15 (unit test 15) passes: one call, for order #42; none for #43.
  7. The mock finds a defect. UT-16 (unit test 16) runs the job at 11:55 and again at 11:56: the mock records two calls for order #42. Debugging shows the cause — nothing remembers that a reminder was sent. Ines opens issue #13; the correction marks each order as reminded; UT-16 (unit test 16) turns green and stays in the suite.
  8. Update the numbers. The code base now has 500 lines and three recorded defects (#11, #12, #13): defect density = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.0 per thousand lines.
Defect report — issue #13: Reminder sent twice for the same order
  • Steps to reproduce: Create order #42 for the 12:00 slot. Run the reminder job at 11:55. Run it again at 11:56.
  • Expected: One reminder for order #42. · Actual: Two reminders for order #42.
  • Version: QueueLess, Sprint 1 build, Python 3.13
  • Severity: 3 — minor (no wrong data; one extra message) · Priority: high (every student who orders receives it, every day)
  • Found by: UT-16 (unit test 16), with the mock notifier · Status: corrected → verified → closed
Defect density: 3 defects ÷ 0.5 KLOC (thousands of lines of code) = 6.0 per thousand lines

Demo 5 — test-first reminders for QueueLess, with a stub and a mock · Python, 387 recorded steps

The task this program does: Runs five TDD (Test-Driven Development) steps — red, green, red, green, refactor — on the reminder rule FR-09 (functional requirement 09) with a tiny test runner; then tests the reminder sender with a stub clock and a mock notifier, lets the mock expose a duplicate reminder, writes the defect report and updates the defect density.

How it relates to the lecture: Lesson 5: the red–green–refactor cycle, Arrange–Act–Assert, stubs and mocks, a defect report with severity and priority, defect density — Lab 07, Steps 1, 6 and 8.

19# FR-09 (functional requirement 09): the reminder is sent when 5 minutes or
20# less remain before the pick-up slot.
21REMINDER_MINUTES = 5
22
23
24# Version 1 — the RED step: the function exists only as a name; calling it
25# raises an error.
26def reminder_due_v1(minutes_left):
27 # Python's way of saying "this behaviour is not written yet".
28 raise NotImplementedError("reminder_due is not written yet")
29
30
31# Version 2 — the first GREEN step: the simplest code that passes the first
32# test.
33def reminder_due_v2(minutes_left):
34 # True when 5 minutes or less remain — but it forgets that the slot may
35 # already have started.
36 return minutes_left <= 5
37
38
39# Version 3 — the second GREEN step: no reminder once the slot has started
40# (negative minutes).
41def reminder_due_v3(minutes_left):
42 # A chained comparison: 0 or more AND 5 or less.
43 return 0 <= minutes_left <= 5
44
45
46# Version 4 — the REFACTOR step: same behaviour, the magic number 5 replaced by
47# the named constant.
48def reminder_due_v4(minutes_left):
49 # Identical results to version 3; easier to read and to change.
50 return 0 <= minutes_left <= REMINDER_MINUTES
51
52
53# The unit tests of FR-09 (functional requirement 09): identifier, name that
54# states the behaviour, input, expected result.
55TESTS = [
56 ("UT-11", "test_reminder_due_five_minutes_before_slot", 5, True),
57 # UT-12 (unit test 12): one minute more than the limit — no reminder.
58 ("UT-12", "test_no_reminder_six_minutes_before_slot", 6, False),
59 # UT-13 (unit test 13): the slot started one minute ago — no reminder.
60 ("UT-13", "test_no_reminder_after_slot_started", -1, False),
61 # UT-14 (unit test 14): the slot starts right now — still a reminder.
62 ("UT-14", "test_reminder_due_when_slot_starts_now", 0, True),
63]
64
65# The five TDD (Test-Driven Development) steps: colour, what the pair does,
66# which version of the code, how many tests exist.
67STEPS = [
68 (
69 "red",
70 "write UT-11 first; the function has no body yet",
71 reminder_due_v1,
72 1,
73 ),
74 # Green: the simplest code; UT-12 (unit test 12) is added and passes at
75 # once.
76 (
77 "green",
78 "simplest code: minutes_left <= 5; add UT-12",
79 reminder_due_v2,
80 2,
81 ),
82 # Red again: UT-13 (unit test 13) describes behaviour the code does not
83 # have yet.
84 (
85 "red",
86 "add UT-13: no reminder once the slot has started",
87 reminder_due_v2,
88 3,
89 ),
90 # Green: correct the rule; UT-14 (unit test 14) is added and passes.
91 ("green", "0 <= minutes_left <= 5; add UT-14", reminder_due_v3, 4),
92 # Refactor: improve the code while every test stays green.
93 ("refactor", "name the constant REMINDER_MINUTES", reminder_due_v4, 4),
94]

96# What the picture on the right shows: the TDD (Test-Driven Development) phase,
97# the test results, the mock's calls, the defect.
98phase = "start"
99# The results of the latest test run.
100results = []
101# The calls recorded by the mock notifier.
102mock_calls = []
103# The defect report, once a test exposes a defect.
104bug = None

106
107# run_tests() is a tiny test runner: it calls the code for each test and
108# compares the result.
109def run_tests(implementation, how_many):
110 # Start a new list of results.
111 results.clear()
112 # Take the first "how_many" tests — the tests that exist at this step.
113 for test_id, name, minutes_left, expected in TESTS[:how_many]:
114 # Act: call the code under test; an exception counts as a failure.
115 try:
116 # The actual result of the code.
117 actual = implementation(minutes_left)
118 # NotImplementedError means the behaviour does not exist yet.
119 except NotImplementedError:
120 # Record the error as the actual result.
121 actual = "NotImplementedError"
122 # Assert: the test passes only if the actual result equals the expected
123 # one.
124 results.append(
125 {
126 "id": test_id,
127 "name": name,
128 "expected": expected,
129 "actual": actual,
130 "ok": actual == expected,
131 }
132 )
133 # The number of passing tests.
134 return sum(1 for r in results if r["ok"])
135
136
137# Run the five TDD (Test-Driven Development) steps one after the other.
138for colour, action, implementation, how_many in STEPS:
139 # Show the current phase in the picture.
140 phase = colour
141 # Run the tests that exist at this step.
142 passed = run_tests(implementation, how_many)
143 # Print the step: colour, action, and how many tests pass.
144 print(f"{colour.upper():8} {action:52} {passed}/{how_many} pass")

147# StubClock is a stub: it returns the time prepared by the test instead of
148# reading the real clock.
149class StubClock:
150 # Store the fixed time (minutes after midnight) given by the test.
151 def __init__(self, minute):
152 # 11:55 is 11 × 60 + 55 = 715.
153 self.minute = minute
154
155 # now() always returns the prepared time.
156 def now(self):
157 # No real clock is involved, so the test gives the same result every
158 # day.
159 return self.minute
160

162# MockNotifier is a mock: it records every call so that the test can check them
163# afterwards.
164class MockNotifier:
165 # notify() would send a message in the real product; here it only records
166 # the order number.
167 def notify(self, order_id, text):
168 # Record the call in the list that the test and the picture read.
169 mock_calls.append(order_id)
170

172# Version 1 of the sender: reminds every order that is due — but remembers
173# nothing.
174def send_due_reminders_v1(orders, clock, notifier):
175 # Look at every order.
176 for order in orders:
177 # If the reminder is due for this order's slot, notify the student.
178 if reminder_due_v4(order["slot"] - clock.now()):
179 # The call that the mock records.
180 notifier.notify(order["id"], "Your order is almost ready")
181
182
183# Version 2 of the sender: the correction — each order is reminded at most
184# once.
185def send_due_reminders_v2(orders, clock, notifier):
186 # Look at every order.
187 for order in orders:
188 # Remind only if it is due AND the order was not reminded before.
189 if (
190 reminder_due_v4(order["slot"] - clock.now())
191 and not order["reminded"]
192 ):
193 # The call that the mock records.
194 notifier.notify(order["id"], "Your order is almost ready")
195 # Remember that this order has been reminded.
196 order["reminded"] = True
197
198
199# test_one() is UT-15 (unit test 15): run the job once at 11:55; only order #42
200# (slot 12:00) is due.
201def test_one(sender):
202 # Arrange: two orders, slots at 12:00 (720) and 12:30 (750), nobody
203 # reminded yet.
204 orders = [
205 {"id": 42, "slot": 720, "reminded": False},
206 {"id": 43, "slot": 750, "reminded": False},
207 ]
208 # Arrange: a fresh mock — clear the calls of any earlier test.
209 mock_calls.clear()
210 # Act: the job runs once, with the stub clock fixed at 11:55 (715).
211 sender(orders, StubClock(715), MockNotifier())
212 # Assert: exactly one call, for order #42; order #43 still has 35 minutes
213 # to go.
214 return mock_calls == [42]
215
216
217# test_once() is UT-16 (unit test 16): run the job at 11:55 and again at 11:56;
218# order #42 must get exactly one reminder.
219def test_once(sender):
220 # Arrange: two orders, slots at 12:00 (720) and 12:30 (750), nobody
221 # reminded yet.
222 orders = [
223 {"id": 42, "slot": 720, "reminded": False},
224 {"id": 43, "slot": 750, "reminded": False},
225 ]
226 # Arrange: a fresh mock — clear the calls of any earlier test.
227 mock_calls.clear()
228 # Act: the job runs at 11:55 (715) …
229 sender(orders, StubClock(715), MockNotifier())
230 # Act: … and again one minute later, at 11:56 (716).
231 sender(orders, StubClock(716), MockNotifier())
232 # Assert: exactly one call, for order #42.
233 return mock_calls == [42]
234
235
236# Doubles, first run: version 1 of the sender.
237phase = "stub + mock"
238# UT-15 (unit test 15) with version 1: one run, one reminder.
239ok_one = test_one(send_due_reminders_v1)

242 f"UT-15 with sender v1: calls {mock_calls} -> "

249 f"UT-16 with sender v1: calls {mock_calls} -> "
250 f"{'pass' if ok_v1 else 'FAIL'}"
251)

254phase = "defect"
255# The fields of a good defect report (Lesson 5).
256bug = {
257 "id": "#13",
258 "title": "Reminder sent twice for the same order",
259 # The steps let anyone reproduce the failure.
260 "steps": "order #42 for 12:00; run the job at 11:55 and at 11:56",
261 # Expected and actual result.
262 "expected": "one reminder",
263 "actual": "two reminders",
264 # Severity: the effect is minor; priority: every student sees it, every

266 "severity": "3 (minor)",
267 "priority": "high",
268 "found by": "UT-16 with the mock notifier",
269}

293# The end of the demo.
294phase = "done"
Execution trace — every step, click one to inspect it
Variables at this step
Output
Step-by-step explanation
  1. Four versions of reminder_due() show the history of the code: v1 has no body yet — it raises NotImplementedError (red), v2 is the simplest code (green), v3 corrects the started-slot case, v4 only renames 5 to REMINDER_MINUTES (refactor).
  2. TESTS are the unit tests UT-11 (unit test 11) to UT-14 (unit test 14): a behaviour name, an input and an expected result each — the boundary values −1, 0, 5 and 6 of FR-09 (functional requirement 09).
  3. run_tests() is a tiny test runner: act (call the code), catch the “not implemented” error, assert (compare). Real frameworks such as pytest do the same with more features.
  4. The five steps print 0/1, 2/2, 2/3, 4/4, 4/4: red, green, red, green, and a refactor that keeps everything green.
  5. StubClock returns a prepared time (11:55 = 715); MockNotifier records every call. The sender is tested without a real clock and without sending messages.
  6. UT-15 (unit test 15) passes with sender v1 (one run, one call). UT-16 (unit test 16) runs the job twice and the mock records two calls for order #42 — the defect.
  7. The defect report #13 has a title, steps, expected and actual results, severity 3 (minor) and priority high — different, on purpose.
  8. Sender v2 remembers which orders were reminded; UT-16 (unit test 16) passes. The density becomes 3 defects ÷ 0.5 KLOC (thousands of lines of code) = 6.0 per thousand lines.

The runner replays the real execution of this program, recorded line by line with Python 3.13; the comment before every line is a teaching format. Download the file and run it yourself with python d5_tdd.py on your own equipment (Legal Notice, section 10 (personal responsibility)↗).

Five flash-cards — turn each one

TDD (Test-Driven Development) — red, green, refactorclick or press Enter to turn
Test-Driven Development: write one failing test (red), write the simplest code that passes (green), improve the code while every test stays green (refactor), and repeat in small steps. Kent Beck, 2002.
unit-test framework and Arrange–Act–Assertclick or press Enter to turn
A framework (pytest, JUnit, Jest) finds the tests, runs them, checks their assertions, prepares fixtures and reports the results. Each test arranges its data, acts by calling the unit once, and asserts the expected result.
stub, mock and fakeclick or press Enter to turn
A stub returns answers prepared by the test (a clock fixed at 11:55) — it controls the unit's inputs. A mock records the calls the unit makes so the test can check them (notify called once, for order 42). A fake is a simplified working version (an in-memory list instead of a database).
severity versus priorityclick or press Enter to turn
Severity: how serious the effect of a defect is (1 critical, 2 major, 3 minor). Priority: how soon it must be corrected (high, medium, low) — a decision of the team and the client. A home-page typo: low severity, high priority.
defect densityclick or press Enter to turn
Defects ÷ KLOC (thousands of lines of code). 12 defects in 3,000 lines → 4 per thousand lines; QueueLess: 3 defects in 500 lines → 6.0. Compare versions and modules of a product, never people.

Self-check — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

⚑ FORMATIVE, NOT SUMMATIVE: this quiz is here to help you learn. It is not recorded, not sent anywhere, and it does NOT count towards your final grade. An MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) has one right answer among four options; an MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) has six options and shows in round brackets how many answers are right.
Question 1Multiple-choice question · four options
In TDD (Test-Driven Development), why must a new test fail before you write the code for it? (one right answer)

💡 Hint: What would a test that has never failed prove?

Question 2Multiple-choice question · four options
QueueLess's send_due_reminders() reads the time from a clock object. In a unit test, the clock always returns 11:55. What is this test double? (one right answer)

💡 Hint: Does it give answers, or does it record calls?

Question 3Multiple-choice question · four options
A crash happens in an export function that no student uses yet; a spelling mistake appears in the title of the home page that every student sees. Which classification fits? (one right answer)

💡 Hint: Severity = how serious; priority = how urgent.

Question 4Multiple-choice question · four options
A team records 9 defects in 4,500 lines of code. What is its defect density? (one right answer)

💡 Hint: Defects ÷ KLOC (thousands of lines of code).

Question 5Multiple-select question · six options
Which items belong in a good defect report? (3 right answers)

💡 Hint: Another person must be able to reproduce the failure without asking you anything.

Question 6Multiple-select question · six options
Which statements about debugging are true? (2 right answers)

💡 Hint: Testing reveals; debugging locates and corrects — step by step.

Lab 08 — announced today, created separately with the Class 8 materials (summary only)

Lab 08 will be the last lab of CS 330. It is not part of today's package: it is created and published separately in the next class, with its own steps, template, time budget and due date. Here is what it will do, so that you can see where today's work goes.

  • Start from your Test Plan v1 of Brick 7 and run, at a small scale, the four types of testing that Brick 7 only plans: integration, system, user acceptance and performance.
  • Integration: two or three tests that join real parts of your product — the controller, the rules, the repository — using a stub or a mock only where a part is not ready.
  • System: a few end-to-end cases taken from the use cases and alternative flows of Brick 5, run in the running product.
  • User acceptance: another team uses your product for its main use case and confirms, or not, that it meets the need.
  • Performance: one simple timing of one operation under a defined load, compared with one non-functional requirement of Brick 5.
  • Record the results and the defects in a short test report that closes the testing of your product before the December 20 deadline.
